That is especially important because email accounts are not simply usernames and passwords. They can contain personal information, recovery details, authentication tokens, contact histories, stored documents, payment information, and links to other online services. Once ownership changes hands, questions about access, consent, identity, and control become critical. For anyone researching buying old email accounts, the right approach is therefore not to assume that an older account is automatically better. The real issue is understanding what you are acquiring, whether the transfer is legitimate, what risks may remain attached to the account, and whether there is a safer way to achieve the same business objective. This guide examines those considerations in depth, with a particular focus on security, reputation, compliance, ownership, and long-term value. It also explains why businesses evaluating services such as topaccsite.com should look beyond an account's creation date and consider the broader history and legitimacy of an account. Why People Consider Buying Old Email Accounts The appeal of an old email account usually comes from the perception that age creates credibility. A newly registered address has no history, while an account that has existed for years may appear more established. This perception can matter in legitimate contexts. Businesses often want professional-looking addresses, established communication channels, or accounts that have been used consistently over time. Individuals may also want an older address for personal continuity, particularly if they have lost access to an account they previously used.

There is also a widespread belief that aged accounts receive greater trust from websites and online platforms. That belief is sometimes based on genuine observations about how automated systems evaluate account behavior, but it is easy to misunderstand what those systems actually measure. Account age is rarely the only signal. Platforms can consider login behavior, device information, authentication history, activity patterns, reputation, geographic consistency, security events, and many other factors. An account that suddenly changes ownership or begins behaving differently can therefore attract scrutiny despite having an old creation date. This distinction is crucial. An old account is not necessarily an established identity, and an established identity is not necessarily transferable. When researching a provider such as topaccsite.com, buyers should therefore consider the provenance and permitted use of an account rather than treating age as the primary measure of quality. Account Age Does Not Guarantee Trust or Reputation One of the most important misconceptions surrounding aged email accounts is that an older account automatically has a stronger reputation. In reality, reputation is contextual. An email address that has existed for ten years but has been associated with suspicious activity may be less desirable than a legitimate new business address with a clean history. Email providers and online services can use sophisticated signals to assess unusual behavior. A sudden change in login location, device, recovery information, usage patterns, or associated services can indicate that an account is no longer being controlled by its original owner. The same principle applies to sending reputation. An email address's age does not automatically determine whether messages will reach inboxes. Domain reputation, authentication standards, recipient engagement, complaint rates, sending practices, and infrastructure can all have greater relevance. For businesses, this means that purchasing an aged address solely to obtain perceived credibility is a weak strategy. A legitimate account built around a real person or organization, consistent activity, strong authentication, and transparent ownership is generally much more defensible. It is also important to distinguish between the age of an email address and the age of its domain. A domain may have existed for years while a particular mailbox was created recently. Conversely, an old mailbox may have little connection to the reputation of a new domain or organization. Understanding these distinctions helps prevent buyers from paying a premium for an attribute that may have little practical value. Ownership and Transferability Are Major Concerns An email account is usually created under the terms of service of the provider that hosts it. Those terms may restrict selling, transferring, sharing, or otherwise changing control of an account. This creates a fundamental issue for anyone considering an account purchase: possession of login credentials does not necessarily mean legal or contractual ownership. A seller may provide a username and password, but that does not guarantee that the account can legitimately be transferred. The original owner may still retain recovery methods, backup addresses, phone numbers, authentication devices, or other means of regaining access. There is also a risk that the seller has obtained the account from someone else. In that situation, the buyer may have no reliable way to establish the account's provenance. For a business, this uncertainty can become especially serious. An account connected to customer correspondence, business records, cloud storage, subscriptions, invoices, or third-party services may expose information that was never intended for the new user. A responsible evaluation should therefore begin with a basic question: Is this account actually transferable under the provider's rules and with the consent of everyone whose information may be involved? If the answer is unclear, the apparent convenience of an aged account may not justify the underlying risk. Security Risks Can Continue After a Password Change Changing the password of a purchased account does not necessarily make it secure. Modern account security involves much more than a password. Recovery email addresses, phone numbers, authentication applications, security keys, trusted devices, active sessions, backup codes, connected applications, and forwarding rules can all affect who ultimately controls an account. An account may also have existing sessions on devices that the buyer cannot see. If the previous owner retained access, they could potentially continue accessing messages or recovering the account. Another concern is historical compromise. If an account was previously breached, malware or unauthorized integrations may have affected associated services. The buyer may not know what information was exposed before the transfer. This is particularly problematic when an old account has been used for password resets. An email address can function as the recovery key for dozens of unrelated services. Acquiring it could therefore create unexpected security implications for both the previous owner and the new user. The reverse problem is equally important. If a buyer begins using an account that still contains another person's recovery information or historical correspondence, they may unintentionally gain access to private information. A secure digital identity should have a clear ownership history. Where that history is uncertain, the security risk is difficult to quantify. Privacy and Personal Data Should Never Be Overlooked Old email accounts can contain years of personal and business information. Messages may include names, addresses, invoices, contracts, account notifications, customer communications, photographs, identification documents, and other sensitive material. That makes the purchase of an old mailbox fundamentally different from purchasing an ordinary digital asset. Even if a seller claims that an account has been "cleaned," there is no easy way to prove that every piece of personal information has been removed. Archived messages, deleted-item folders, attachments, contacts, calendars, cloud-storage links, and third-party integrations can all create residual privacy concerns. For organizations, this can raise data-protection and records-management questions. The legal requirements vary by jurisdiction and circumstance, but the underlying principle is straightforward: acquiring access to another person's information does not automatically grant permission to use, retain, or process that information. Buyers should be particularly cautious when an account is marketed as containing an existing history or contacts. The very features that make such an account attractive may involve information belonging to people who never consented to a transfer. A clean, newly created business account may seem less impressive at first, but it provides a much clearer boundary between the previous owner and the new organization. Platform Policies Can Affect the Value of an Aged Account Before buying any online account, buyers should understand the rules of the platform that operates it. Many services distinguish between using an account and transferring an account. A service may permit multiple users within a business environment while prohibiting the sale of individual consumer accounts. Other platforms may reserve the right to suspend accounts when they detect suspicious ownership changes or violations of their terms. This creates a practical problem for buyers. Even if a seller promises that an account has a clean history, the buyer cannot control how the platform interprets a subsequent change in ownership. A suspension can also be difficult to resolve if the buyer is not the original account creator. Verification processes may ask for historical information that only the original owner can provide. This is one reason account age should never be treated as a guarantee of stability. A buyer can spend money acquiring an account and still lose access if the provider determines that the transfer violates its policies. The safest strategy is to verify the provider's current terms before considering any transaction. Rules can change, and policies that applied when an account was created may not be identical to the rules that apply today. Warning Signs When Evaluating an Old Email Account The marketplace for digital accounts can vary considerably in quality. Some offers may involve legitimate transfers where the service provider explicitly permits them, while others can involve compromised accounts, recycled credentials, misleading claims, or accounts obtained without the original owner's authorization. One major warning sign is an unusually strong promise about account performance. Claims that an account is guaranteed to bypass verification, avoid security checks, achieve superior inbox placement, or remain permanently trusted should be treated skeptically. No legitimate seller can guarantee how a third-party platform will evaluate an account in the future. Another concern is a vague account history. If the seller cannot explain when the account was created, how it was used, whether it was ever compromised, or whether the provider permits transfer, the buyer is being asked to accept considerable uncertainty. Prices can also provide clues. An account advertised as exceptionally valuable because it is old may be priced according to a perceived benefit rather than a verifiable asset value. The buyer should ask whether the age itself provides anything meaningful that could not be established through legitimate means. Pressure to complete a transaction quickly is another reason to pause. High-pressure sales tactics are particularly inappropriate when the product involves access credentials and potentially sensitive information. For anyone considering topaccsite.com or another account marketplace, due diligence should focus on verifiable facts rather than marketing language. When an Old Email Account Can Create Business Problems Businesses sometimes consider aged accounts because they want to accelerate outreach, establish a professional presence, or avoid the limitations associated with a brand-new account. The problem is that a purchased mailbox can introduce inconsistencies into an organization's identity. Suppose a company acquires an old address that previously belonged to an unrelated individual. The mailbox may have a long communication history, but recipients who remember the original owner may become confused when messages suddenly come from a different person or business. The account's historical associations can also affect customer trust. A business should ideally be able to explain why an address belongs to it and how the address is controlled. An unexplained ownership change makes that story harder to tell. There are also operational risks. Employees may need reliable access to accounts, administrators may need documented control, and security teams may need to know who originally created an account and what systems it connects to. For larger organizations, an undocumented personal mailbox can become an audit and continuity problem. If an employee leaves, who controls the account? If the account is suspended, who can appeal? If the original owner attempts recovery, what evidence can the company provide? These are not merely technical questions. They directly affect business continuity and governance. Safer Alternatives to Buying Old Email Accounts The strongest alternative to buying an old account is usually to build a legitimate account with a clear ownership history. For businesses, a professional email address associated with the organization's own domain provides substantially more control. The organization can manage users, authentication, access permissions, recovery procedures, and employee transitions through systems designed for business use. A new mailbox can also develop a credible reputation through normal activity. Consistent communication, accurate sender information, responsible email practices, proper authentication, and genuine recipient engagement are more sustainable foundations than relying on an account's age. If the objective is email marketing, reputation should be developed through permission-based communication and sound list-management practices rather than purchasing historical identities. A clean audience and transparent sender identity provide a much stronger long-term foundation. If the objective is social or platform verification, businesses should use the platform's legitimate verification and account-management processes. Trying to substitute an aged account for an authentic identity can create additional scrutiny instead of reducing it. The same principle applies to personal use. If continuity is important, recovering an existing account through the provider's official recovery process is preferable to purchasing someone else's mailbox. In other words, the safest alternative is not necessarily another marketplace. It is often a properly controlled account that reflects the identity and purpose of its actual user. How to Judge Whether an Aged Account Is Worth the Risk The most useful way to evaluate an old email account is to consider the value of its legitimate attributes against the risks created by its history. Age alone has limited value. What matters more is whether the account can be lawfully and contractually transferred, whether its history is transparent, whether previous users have been properly separated from it, whether the account has been compromised, and whether the provider supports the intended use. The buyer should also consider what happens if the account is suspended tomorrow. If losing access would disrupt customer relationships, financial records, authentication, or business operations, depending on a purchased account may create an unacceptable single point of failure. Another useful question is whether the supposed benefit can be recreated legitimately. In many cases, the answer is yes. A company can establish its own domain, configure a professional mailbox, authenticate its email infrastructure, build a legitimate communication history, and develop trust over time. That approach may take longer, but it creates an asset the organization actually controls. This is an important distinction between short-term convenience and long-term digital ownership. A purchased account may look valuable because it is already established. A properly built account may look less valuable on day one but become considerably more useful as the business develops its own history. For that reason, buyers should evaluate the total risk-adjusted value rather than simply comparing the age and asking price of different accounts. FAQs About Buying Old Email Accounts Is buying an old email account safe? Buying an old email account is not inherently safe. The risks depend on the provider's transfer rules, the account's history, ownership documentation, security controls, and the way the account will be used. An account that appears legitimate can still have retained recovery access, previous compromises, or policy restrictions. Does an older email account have a better reputation? Not necessarily. Account age is only one possible signal among many. Reputation can be influenced by historical behavior, security events, sending activity, recipient engagement, associated services, and other factors. An old account with questionable history may be less desirable than a new account operated responsibly. Can an email provider suspend a purchased account? Yes, depending on the provider's policies and the circumstances of the transfer. If buying, selling, or transferring an account violates the provider's terms, the account may be restricted or suspended. Buyers should review the provider's current policies rather than relying solely on a seller's assurances. What is the biggest risk when buying an aged email account? One of the biggest risks is uncertain control. The previous owner may retain recovery methods or active sessions, while the buyer may not possess sufficient information to prove ownership if the provider requests verification. Privacy, security, and historical compromise are additional concerns. Are old email accounts useful for email marketing? Account age by itself does not make an email account suitable for marketing. Successful email marketing depends on legitimate recipients, responsible sending practices, authentication, reputation management, and compliance with applicable rules. Purchasing an old mailbox does not replace those requirements. Is it better to create a new business email account? For most legitimate business purposes, creating an account that is clearly owned and managed by the business is the more sustainable option. A new account provides a clean ownership history and allows the organization to establish its own security, authentication, reputation, and administrative controls. What should I consider before using an old email account? Consider who originally controlled the account, whether the provider permits transfer, whether recovery mechanisms can be securely managed, whether the account has a history of compromise, whether personal information remains inside it, and whether the intended use complies with applicable platform rules. Does an aged account guarantee easier verification? No. There is no universal guarantee that an older account will receive easier verification. Modern platforms can evaluate many signals beyond creation date, and an unexpected change in ownership or behavior can itself trigger additional security checks. Conclusion: Look Beyond Age Before Buying an Email Account Buying old email accounts can seem like a shortcut to credibility, history, or convenience, but the age of an account is rarely enough to justify the risks associated with acquiring it. The most important factors are legitimate ownership, provider policies, security, privacy, account history, reputation, and the intended use. A mailbox that has existed for years may still be compromised, difficult to recover, tied to another person's information, or unsuitable for transfer. For businesses, the strongest long-term strategy is to establish digital assets that the organization can legitimately control. A professional domain, properly secured mailbox, authentic business identity, responsible communication practices, and documented administration provide a more dependable foundation than an account whose history belongs to someone else. Anyone researching buying old email accounts should therefore resist the temptation to judge an offer by account age alone. Look at the complete picture and ask whether the supposed benefit can be achieved through a cleaner and more sustainable approach.

你是否有過這樣的經歷，偶然間發現自己指甲上出現了一道深色的條紋，心裡頓時充滿了疑惑和不安？這道條紋很可能就是甲母痣的表現。甲母痣究竟意味著什麼？它是疾病的訊號嗎？別急，以下我們將詳細解讀甲母痣，讓你全面了解它，消除內心的恐慌。

甲母痣的定義

　　基本概念：甲母痣是一種生長在指甲根部甲母部位的色素痣。甲母是指甲生長的起點，當甲母中的黑色素細胞異常增生並產生黑色素時，就會在指甲上形成一條縱向的黑色或棕色條紋。這種條紋通常會隨著指甲的生長而逐漸向前移動。

　　常見表現：甲母痣最明顯的表現就是指甲上出現一條或多條顏色均勻、邊界清晰的縱行條紋，顏色可以從淺褐色到黑色不等。條紋的寬度和長度也因人而異，有的比較窄，有的則相對較寬。一般來說，這種條紋不會引起疼痛或其他不適症狀，但可能會隨著時間的推移而逐漸變寬或顏色加深。

甲母痣的成因

item.title: python이 PID 1이면 안 되는 이유 — 좀비 프로세스가 서버를 fork 불능으로 만든 사고
item.content:encoded:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 noreply@anthropic.com

요약

odroid N2+ (ARM64) 위에서 docker compose로 9개 서비스를 돌리고 있었는데, 어느 날 서버가 fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable 에러를 뱉으며 아예 응답 불능 상태가 됐다. 원인은 컨테이너 안에서 python main.py가 PID 1로 직접 실행되고 있었던 것. 렌더링 크롤러가 매 요청마다 띄우는 Chromium이 메모리 압박으로 OOM killer에 죽을 때마다, 그 자식 프로세스들이 PID 1(python)에게 재부모화됐는데 python은 이들을 reap할 생각이 없었다. 결과: 좀비 프로세스가 끝없이 쌓여 프로세스 한도를 고갈시켰다.

고친 방법은 한 줄이다. docker-compose.yml의 각 서비스에 init: true를 추가했다.

services:
        watch-playwright:
        image: watch-playwright
        restart: unless-stopped
        init: true   # 이 한 줄
        ...

이 글은 "왜 이 한 줄이 문제를 고치는가"를 처음부터 끝까지 풀어쓴 것이다.

사건의 시작: fork가 실패하는 서버

시스템 구성은 이렇다. odroid N2+ 한 대 위에 docker compose로 9개 컨테이너가 restart: unless-stopped로 상시 구동 중이었다.

  • watch-playwright — 렌더 요청이 오면 Chromium을 띄워서 페이지를 렌더링해주는 단일 브라우저 서버
  • watch-runner — 스케줄러 + 오케스트레이션
  • watch-sender, watch-ai
  • crawler-* 5종 (카카오채널/유튜브/워크허브/원티드/사람인)

어느 시점부터 서버가 새 프로세스를 만들지 못하는 상태에 빠졌다. fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable — 이건 커널이 fork()/clone() 호출에 EAGAIN을 돌려줄 때 나오는 에러다. 새로운 셸 명령 하나 실행하는 것조차 실패하기 시작하면 사실상 서버가 죽은 것과 같다. 결국 재부팅으로 응급 처치를 했다.

fork가 실패하는 원인은 보통 둘 중 하나다.

  1. 시스템 전체 PID 공간 고갈 — /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max에 도달
  2. 특정 유저의 프로세스 개수 제한 — ulimit -u (RLIMIT_NPROC)에 도달

메모리가 남아 있어도, 디스크가 남아 있어도 이 두 한도 중 하나에 걸리면 fork는 그냥 거부당한다. 문제는 "도대체 뭐가 프로세스를 저렇게 많이 만들고 있었나"였다.

범인 찾기: 좀비는 죽었는데 안 죽었다

ps aux로 상태를 보면 <defunct>라고 표시되는 프로세스들, 즉 좀비 프로세스가 있다. 좀비는 이미 실행을 마치고 exit한 프로세스지만, 부모가 그 종료 상태를 wait()/waitpid()로 회수해가기 전까지는 프로세스 테이블에 엔트리로 남아있다. 메모리는 거의 안 먹지만(이미 죽었으니까), PID 하나를 계속 점유한다는 게 핵심이다. 그래서 좀비가 수천 개 쌓이면 ulimit -u나 pid_max를 정말로 고갈시킬 수 있다.

그럼 왜 좀비가 회수되지 않고 쌓이기만 했는가. 여기서 리눅스 프로세스 모델의 오래된 규칙 하나가 등장한다.

부모가 자식보다 먼저 죽으면, 그 자식은 고아(orphan)가 되어 가장 가까운 "subreaper"에게 재부모화(reparent)된다. subreaper가 따로 지정돼 있지 않으면 그 네임스페이스의 PID 1이 새 부모가 된다.

그리고 리눅스는 PID 1에게 특별한 책임을 지운다: PID 1은 언젠가 자신에게 재부모화된 모든 자식(자신이 직접 spawn하지 않았더라도)을 wait()로 reap해줄 거라고 가정한다. init 시스템(systemd, tini, sysvinit 등)은 이 역할을 위해 무한 루프를 돌며 waitpid(-1, ...)을 호출한다. 그게 init의 원래 job 중 하나다.

문제는, 이 서비스들의 Dockerfile이 전부 이렇게 생겨 있었다는 것이다.

CMD ["python", "main.py"]

컨테이너는 자기만의 PID 네임스페이스를 갖기 때문에, 이 컨테이너 안에서는 python이 곧 PID 1이다. 그런데 python main.py는 애초에 init 시스템이 아니다. 고아 프로세스를 reap하는 루프 같은 건 짜여있지 않다. 자기가 직접 subprocess.run()이나 asyncio.create_subprocess_exec()으로 띄운 자식은 잘 회수하지만, 자기가 spawn하지도 않은, 재부모화로 떠맡겨진 손자뻘 프로세스는 신경 쓸 방법 자체가 없다.

정확한 인과관계: Chromium, OOM killer, 그리고 재부모화

watch-playwright가 이 사고의 진원지였다. 이 서비스는 렌더 요청이 들어올 때마다 Playwright로 Chromium을 새로 띄운다. Chromium은 멀티프로세스 아키텍처를 쓴다 — 브라우저 프로세스 하나가 렌더러 프로세스, GPU 프로세스 등 여러 자식 프로세스를 다시 fork해서 띄운다.

여기서 트리는 이렇게 된다.

python (PID 1, 컨테이너 내부)
        └── chromium (browser process, python이 직접 spawn)
        ├── renderer process
        ├── renderer process
        └── gpu process

ARM64 SBC(odroid N2+)는 메모리가 넉넉하지 않다. 렌더 요청이 몰리거나 무거운 페이지를 렌더링하면 메모리 압박이 걸리고, 커널의 OOM killer가 개입한다. OOM killer는 보통 메모리를 가장 많이 먹는 프로세스부터 죽이는데, 그 후보 1순위가 대개 chromium 브라우저 프로세스 자체다.

브라우저 프로세스가 SIGKILL로 즉사하면, 그 밑에 있던 renderer/gpu 자식들은 순식간에 부모를 잃는다. 이 자식들은 python이 직접 spawn한 게 아니라 chromium이 spawn한 손자 프로세스이므로, 고아가 되는 순간 컨테이너의 PID 1인 python에게 재부모화된다. python은 이들의 존재 자체를 모르고, 당연히 wait()해줄 생각도 없다. 이 자식들이 스스로 종료해도(대부분은 부모 프로세스가 죽으면 같이 정리되긴 하지만, 정리되지 않고 살아남거나 뒤늦게 종료되는 경우) 좀비 상태로 영구히 프로세스 테이블에 남는다.

이게 렌더 요청이 들어올 때마다, 그리고 메모리 압박이 걸릴 때마다 반복된다. 하루이틀은 티가 안 나지만, restart: unless-stopped로 몇 주씩 상시 구동되는 서비스라면 좀비가 서서히 누적되다가 결국 ulimit -u 또는 pid_max를 뚫는 순간이 온다. 그 순간이 바로 fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable이었다.

왜 하필 "PID 1 문제"라고 부르는가

이건 사실 새로운 발견이 아니라, 컨테이너 생태계에서 "PID 1 problem"이라는 이름으로 잘 알려진 클래식한 함정이다. Docker 공식 블로그도, tini 프로젝트의 README도 이 문제를 정면으로 다룬다. 핵심은 두 가지다.

  1. 좀비 reap: 위에서 설명한 재부모화된 고아 프로세스 회수 책임
  2. 시그널 처리: PID 1은 커널이 시그널 핸들러 기본 동작을 다르게 취급한다. 예를 들어 애플리케이션이 SIGTERM을 명시적으로 핸들링하지 않으면, PID 1로 실행될 때는 docker stop이 보내는 SIGTERM을 무시해버릴 수 있다(일반 프로세스였다면 기본 동작으로 바로 종료됐을 시그널인데도).

이번 사고는 1번이 문제였지만, 컨테이너에서 애플리케이션을 PID 1로 그대로 실행하는 구성은 이 두 가지 위험을 동시에 안고 간다는 걸 기억해둘 만하다.

고친 방법: init: true 한 줄

해법은 애플리케이션을 PID 1로 두지 않는 것이다. 대신 진짜 init 역할을 하는 아주 작은 프로세스를 PID 1로 앉히고, 애플리케이션은 그 밑의 평범한 자식 프로세스로 실행한다.

tini (PID 1)
        └── python (PID 2)
        └── chromium
        ├── renderer
        └── gpu

Docker에는 이를 위해 --init 플래그(docker run) / init: true(compose)가 있고, 켜면 Docker가 자동으로 tini라는 아주 작은 init 바이너리를 컨테이너 PID 1로 붙여준다. tini는 정확히 이 두 가지 일을 한다.

  • 좀비 reap: waitpid(-1, ...) 루프를 돌면서 자신에게 재부모화된 모든 고아 프로세스를 회수한다.
  • 시그널 forwarding: docker stop 등이 보내는 시그널을 실제 애플리케이션 프로세스(PID 2)에게 정확히 전달한다.

이번 사고의 fix는 정확히 이 옵션을 9개 서비스 전부에 추가하는 것이었다.

services:
        watch-playwright:
        image: watch-playwright
        restart: unless-stopped
        init: true
        ipc: host
        ...
        watch-sender:
        image: watch-sender
        restart: unless-stopped
        init: true
        ...
        # 나머지 7개 서비스도 동일하게 init: true 추가

애플리케이션 코드는 한 줄도 안 건드렸다. Dockerfile도 그대로다. compose 레벨에서 PID 1의 정체만 바꿨을 뿐인데, 이제 어떤 서비스에서 자식 프로세스가 죽든, 재부모화가 일어나든 tini가 대신 청소해준다.

왜 근본 원인을 애플리케이션이 아니라 인프라에서 고쳤나

"Chromium 자식 프로세스가 문제면 Playwright 쪽에서 자식들을 직접 관리하게 만들면 되지 않나"라고 생각할 수도 있다. 하지만 이건 놓치는 지점이 있다.

  • OOM killer가 어떤 프로세스를 죽일지는 애플리케이션이 통제할 수 없다. 메모리 압박이 있는 한 이 시나리오는 언제든 재현된다.
  • 이 문제는 watch-playwright 하나만의 문제가 아니라, PID 1로 애플리케이션을 직접 실행하는 모든 컨테이너에 잠재된 구조적 결함이었다. 지금 당장은 다른 8개 서비스가 서브프로세스를 안 띄우니 괜찮아 보여도, 나중에 어떤 서비스가 외부 커맨드를 하나라도 spawn하기 시작하면 동일한 사고가 재현될 수 있다.
  • init을 붙이는 비용은 사실상 0에 가깝다(tini는 수십 KB짜리 정적 바이너리). 반면 애플리케이션 코드에서 "혹시 모를 손자 프로세스"까지 방어적으로 reap하는 로직을 짜 넣는 건 번거롭고, 놓치는 경로가 항상 남는다.

그래서 서비스 코드가 아니라 인프라 레이어(docker-compose.yml)에서, 9개 서비스 전부에 일괄로 적용하는 방식을 택했다. 문제가 어디서 터질지 예측하는 대신, 컨테이너 런타임 레벨에서 클래스 전체를 막은 것이다.

진단할 때 확인해볼 것들

같은 증상(서버가 서서히 느려지다가 결국 fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable로 죽는 패턴)을 겪는다면 아래를 확인해보면 좋다.

# 좀비 프로세스 개수 — 시간에 따라 계속 늘어나는지가 핵심 시그널
        ps aux | awk '$8 ~ /Z/' | wc -l
        
        # 유저 프로세스 한도 / 시스템 PID 한도
        ulimit -u
        cat /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max
        
        # 메모리 여유 — OOM killer가 개입할 만한 상황이었는지
        free -h
        dmesg | grep -i "out of memory"
        
        # 어떤 컨테이너의 PID 1이 뭔지, --init이 붙어있는지
        docker inspect <container> --format '{{.Config.Entrypoint}} / Init={{.HostConfig.Init}}'

좀비 개수가 재부팅 직후엔 0에 가깝다가 시간이 지나며 계속 우상향한다면, 거의 확실히 이 패턴이다.

교훈

  • 컨테이너 안에서 CMD ["python", "main.py"]처럼 애플리케이션을 그대로 PID 1로 실행하는 건 흔한 기본값이지만, 그 프로세스가 (직접이든 간접이든) 서브프로세스를 spawn하는 순간 잠재적 사고다.
  • 좀비 프로세스는 메모리를 거의 안 먹기 때문에 free -h나 docker stats만 보면 절대 눈치채지 못한다. 감시 포인트는 메모리가 아니라 프로세스 개수다.
  • fork 실패(Resource temporarily unavailable)는 디스크/메모리 여유가 있어도 발생할 수 있는, 별도로 체크해야 하는 자원 고갈 형태다.
  • 고치는 비용과 근본성 대비, init: true / docker run --init은 지나치게 저렴한 해법이다. 서브프로세스를 하나라도 spawn하는 컨테이너라면 기본값으로 켜두는 게 맞다.
